Reliability profiles and their summaries

Source: vignettes/reliability-profiles.Rmd
reliability-profiles.Rmd

Two trials can have the same informativeness and still differ in what partial pooling does to their sites. In one, every site is about equally reliable. In another, a few precise sites stand next to many noisy ones. In this vignette we take the between-site standard deviation στ\sigma_\tau as known and study the reliabilities themselves. We look at how the informativeness averages them, what the dispersion and the concentration count add, and how all four summaries change with στ\sigma_\tau, using the geometry of Lee (2026) without deriving it.

library(poolinfo)

Site jj’s reliability is Sj=στ2/(στ2+vj)S_j = \sigma_\tau^2 / (\sigma_\tau^2 + v_j), where vjv_j is the sampling variance of the site’s estimate, and a trial’s reliability profile is the set of its JJ reliabilities. See vignette("poolinfo") for why SjS_j is both a reliability and the shrinkage weight of the normal model.

Five profiles with the same informativeness

Our examples come from the data set example_profiles, with the sampling variances of five artificial trials of 40 sites each and the reliabilities that they give at στ=0.2\sigma_\tau = 0.2. All five have the informativeness I=0.3I = 0.3. They differ in their logit variance VV, the variance of the logits logitSj\mathrm{logit}\, S_j with divisor JJ. Because logitSj=log⁡στ2−log⁡vj\mathrm{logit}\, S_j = \log\sigma_\tau^2 - \log v_j, VV is also the variance of the log sampling variances, and it does not change with στ\sigma_\tau. The five profiles are

  • homogeneous, in which every site has the same sampling variance, so that V=0V = 0;
  • even, with log variances spread evenly;
  • bimodal, with two groups of 20 sites, one precise and one noisy;
  • concentrated_precise, with 8 precise sites and 32 noisy ones;
  • concentrated_noisy, with 32 precise sites and 8 noisy ones.

Apart from homogeneous, all have V=1.5V = 1.5. R’s var() divides by J−1J - 1 instead and gives 1.54 for them.

We make a profile of each trial with reliability_profile(), from its sampling variances and στ\sigma_\tau, and collect the five profiles with compare_profiles().

by_shape <- split(example_profiles, example_profiles$profile)
profiles <- lapply(by_shape, function(d) {
  reliability_profile(se2 = d$se2, sigma_tau = 0.2)
})
cmp <- compare_profiles(.list = profiles)
cmp
#> Comparison of 5 analyses
#> Each analysis is conditional on its own standard errors.
#> 
#>   analysis              J   informativeness I  mean reliability
#>   homogeneous           40  0.300              0.300
#>   even                  40  0.300              0.347
#>   bimodal               40  0.300              0.353
#>   concentrated_precise  40  0.300              0.317
#>   concentrated_noisy    40  0.300              0.360
#> 
#>   analysis              dispersion H  concentration count J_eff
#>   homogeneous           0.0000        40.0
#>   even                  0.1486        27.6
#>   bimodal               0.1524        27.3
#>   concentrated_precise  0.1676        24.1
#>   concentrated_noisy    0.1166        33.3

In every row I=0.300I = 0.300, while the mean reliability runs from 0.300 in the homogeneous profile to 0.360. Although the four unequal profiles have the same logit variance, their dispersions range from 0.117 to 0.168 and their concentration counts from 24.1 to 33.3, against 0 and 40 for the homogeneous profile. Of the four, the profile with 8 noisy sites has the smallest dispersion and yet the largest mean reliability, 0.360. Its mirror image, with 8 precise sites, combines the largest dispersion with the smallest mean reliability among them, 0.317. So a larger dispersion need not come with a larger gap between the mean reliability and II(Lee 2026). In every column the even and bimodal profiles are close to each other.

Sorting the reliabilities of the two concentrated profiles shows where these differences come from. We put the two in one comparison, to use again below, and plot their sorted reliabilities in one panel.

two <- compare_profiles(
  `8 precise` = profiles$concentrated_precise,
  `8 noisy` = profiles$concentrated_noisy
)
plot(two, type = "profile")

With 8 precise sites, the other 32 sit together at 0.19, below II, and the precise ones at 0.83. In the profile with 8 noisy sites it is the other way around, with 32 sites at 0.44, above II, and 8 at 0.04. In each profile the few sites lie far from II on the logit scale and the many lie close to it on the other side, so that the logits average to logitI\mathrm{logit}\, I.

Three averages of the reliabilities

On the logit scale, the informativeness is the plain average of the reliabilities,

logitI=1J∑j=1JlogitSj,I=στ2στ2+GM(v), \mathrm{logit}\, I = \frac{1}{J}\sum_{j=1}^J \mathrm{logit}\, S_j, \qquad I = \frac{\sigma_\tau^2}{\sigma_\tau^2 + \mathrm{GM}(v)},

where GM(v)\mathrm{GM}(v) is the geometric mean of the sampling variances. Because the logits are log⁡στ2−log⁡vj\log\sigma_\tau^2 - \log v_j, averaging them averages the log variances, which gives the second form.

Lee (2026, Theorem 1) shows that II is also the value pp that minimizes the average Kullback-Leibler divergence

1J∑j=1JKL{Ber(p)∥Ber(Sj)}. \frac{1}{J}\sum_{j=1}^J \mathrm{KL}\{\mathrm{Ber}(p) \,\|\, \mathrm{Ber}(S_j)\}.

We call the minimizer of such an average a centroid of the reliabilities. This divergence is one of the Bregman divergences, and two others give the other familiar means. With pp in the first argument, as above, squared error gives the arithmetic mean S‾\bar S, and the Bregman divergence of the Burg potential −log⁡p-\log p gives the harmonic mean, our harmonic centroid. With pp in the second argument, all three divergences give S‾\bar S. reliability_centroids() returns the three first-argument centroids, and we apply it to each profile.

centroids <- sapply(by_shape, function(d) reliability_centroids(d$reliability))
round(t(centroids), 3)
#>                      harmonic   I  mean
#> homogeneous             0.300 0.3 0.300
#> even                    0.181 0.3 0.347
#> bimodal                 0.188 0.3 0.353
#> concentrated_precise    0.223 0.3 0.317
#> concentrated_noisy      0.135 0.3 0.360

In the four unequal profiles the harmonic centroid, from 0.135 to 0.223, lies below II. It is never larger than the other two, in any profile, and the three are equal only when all the reliabilities are, as in the homogeneous profile. Between II and S‾\bar S, however, there is no general order. Here S‾>I\bar S > I in all four unequal profiles, the sign of 1−2I1 - 2I. A profile close enough to constant must have that sign when I≠1/2I \ne 1/2, but a profile far from constant can have the other. Lee (2026) gives one with 25 sites and I=0.3I = 0.3, where one site is far more precise than the other 24, which are all alike. We build it from its centered logits Δj=logitSj−logitI\Delta_j = \mathrm{logit}\, S_j - \mathrm{logit}\, I, with mean 0 and variance V=2V = 2.

delta <- c(sqrt(48), rep(-sqrt(1 / 12), 24))
S <- plogis(qlogis(0.3) + delta)
reliability_centroids(S)
#>  harmonic         I      mean 
#> 0.2506438 0.3000000 0.2732468

Its mean reliability, 0.273, is below II although I<1/2I < 1/2. In the next section we give a condition that guarantees the sign of 1−2I1 - 2I.

The dispersion and the gap between the averages

The dispersion HH is the smallest value of the average divergence above, reached at p=Ip = I,

H=1J∑j=1JKL{Ber(I)∥Ber(Sj)}, H = \frac{1}{J}\sum_{j=1}^J \mathrm{KL}\{\mathrm{Ber}(I) \,\|\, \mathrm{Ber}(S_j)\},

the average divergence of II from the site reliabilities. It is 0 only for a constant profile.

The sign of the gap S‾−I\bar S - I matters for the site effects. If στ\sigma_\tau and the mean effect were known, the normal model would give the site effects an average posterior variance of στ2(1−S‾)\sigma_\tau^2(1 - \bar S)(Lee 2026, Proposition 2). Equally reliable sites with the same II would give στ2(1−I)\sigma_\tau^2(1 - I), so a positive gap means a smaller average posterior variance than theirs, and a negative gap a larger one.

Both HH and the gap have leading terms proportional to the logit variance VV. With ρ3=J−1∑j|Δj|3\rho_3 = J^{-1}\sum_j |\Delta_j|^3, the third absolute moment of the centered logits, Proposition 2 of Lee (2026) gives

H=12I(1−I)V+RH,|RH|≤3108ρ3,S‾−I=12I(1−I)(1−2I)V+RS,|RS|≤148ρ3. \begin{aligned} H &= \tfrac12 I(1-I)V + R_H, & |R_H| &\le \tfrac{\sqrt3}{108}\,\rho_3,\\ \bar S - I &= \tfrac12 I(1-I)(1-2I)V + R_S, & |R_S| &\le \tfrac{1}{48}\,\rho_3. \end{aligned}

When the gap’s leading term is larger than its bound in absolute value, the gap has the sign of 1−2I1 - 2I. local_terms() gives, for HH and for the gap, the exact value, the leading term and the bound, and a logical column, holds, that is TRUE when the leading term is the larger. We look first at the bimodal profile.

local_terms(by_shape$bimodal$reliability)
#>   quantity      exact leading      bound holds
#> 1        H 0.15241610  0.1575 0.02946278  TRUE
#> 2      gap 0.05255058  0.0630 0.03827328  TRUE

For this profile the gap’s leading term, 0.063, is larger than its bound, 0.038, so the gap is positive, as 1−2I1 - 2I is, and its exact value is 0.053. Since HH is never negative, its bound measures instead how close the leading term is. Here H=0.152H = 0.152, within 0.030 of 0.158.

With 8 precise sites the leading terms are the same, because II and VV are, but a few of the centered logits are large, and ρ3\rho_3 rises from 1.84 to 3.12.

local_terms(by_shape$concentrated_precise$reliability)
#>   quantity      exact leading      bound holds
#> 1        H 0.16758423  0.1575 0.05008673  TRUE
#> 2      gap 0.01727911  0.0630 0.06506457 FALSE

Now the gap’s bound, 0.065, is larger than its leading term, 0.063, and holds is FALSE, so the leading term alone does not fix the sign. The gap is still positive, but at 0.017 it is only 27% of the leading term. Its remainder, -0.046, cancels most of the leading term and comes from the 8 precise sites, whose logits lie far above the rest. In the profile of 25 sites the bound is 0.278, more than three times the leading term, and there the remainder reverses the sign.

Site jj’s term of HH, KL{Ber(I)∥Ber(Sj)}\mathrm{KL}\{\mathrm{Ber}(I) \,\|\, \mathrm{Ber}(S_j)\}, is the divergence of II from that site’s reliability. kl_contributions() returns the terms, and plot_contributions() plots them in increasing order, here for the profile with 8 precise sites.

plot_contributions(profiles$concentrated_precise)

Each of the 8 precise sites has a term of 0.694, against 0.036 for each of the other 32, so these 8 sites account for 83% of HH.

Changing the between-site standard deviation

The sampling variances fix the centered logits, Δj=log⁡GM(v)−log⁡vj\Delta_j = \log \mathrm{GM}(v) - \log v_j, and στ\sigma_\tau moves all the logits together. As στ\sigma_\tau grows from 0, II grows from 0 to 1, and along this path the derivative of HH with respect to the logit of II is the gap S‾−I\bar S - I(Lee 2026, Proposition 2). So HH rises from 0 while the mean reliability is above II, reaches its largest value where the gap is 0, and falls back to 0. To see how far the summaries move, we compute the profile with 8 precise sites at four values of στ\sigma_\tau with update().

precise <- profiles$concentrated_precise
sigmas <- c(0.15, 0.2, 0.25, 0.3)
along <- sapply(sigmas, function(s) {
  update(precise, sigma_tau = s)$stats[c("I", "mean", "gap", "H", "J_eff")]
})
round(cbind(sigma_tau = sigmas, t(along)), 3)
#>      sigma_tau     I  mean    gap     H  J_eff
#> [1,]      0.15 0.194 0.240  0.045 0.149 19.298
#> [2,]      0.20 0.300 0.317  0.017 0.168 24.114
#> [3,]      0.25 0.401 0.390 -0.011 0.169 28.505
#> [4,]      0.30 0.491 0.458 -0.033 0.161 31.959

Over this range HH stays between 0.149 and 0.169, while the gap changes sign, from 0.045 to -0.033, and the concentration count rises from 19.3 to 32.0. At στ=0.25\sigma_\tau = 0.25 the mean reliability, 0.390, is below I=0.401I = 0.401 although I<1/2I < 1/2, as in the profile of 25 sites.

profile_path() follows the whole path with the centered logits held fixed, and for a profile it also gives στ\sigma_\tau at each point. On a fine grid we find where HH is largest.

path <- profile_path(precise, n = 2001)
path[which.max(path$H), c("sigma_tau", "I", "H", "gap")]
#>     sigma_tau         I         H          gap
#> 723 0.2296954 0.3611389 0.1700047 1.607891e-06

At the peak, H=0.170H = 0.170, στ≈0.23\sigma_\tau \approx 0.23 and I≈0.36I \approx 0.36, and the gap is 0 up to the spacing of the grid. So the peak is not at I=1/2I = 1/2, where the gap’s leading term changes sign. plot_gap_path() plots HH and the gap along the path, with their leading terms.

plot_gap_path(precise)

In the left panel HH rises steeply from 0, peaks at the cross and returns to 0 at I=1I = 1, while its leading term (dashed) peaks at I=1/2I = 1/2. In the right panel the gap crosses 0 at the same II, about 0.36, and stays negative up to I=1I = 1. For every II strictly between this peak and 1/2, this profile has S‾<I\bar S < I, against the sign of its leading term. The point on each curve is the profile at στ=0.2\sigma_\tau = 0.2, before the peak. A much larger στ\sigma_\tau would bring all the reliabilities close to 1, where HH and the gap return to 0. Along every path with unequal sampling variances the gap changes sign once, because HH is strictly concave in II when the centered logits are fixed. With equal sampling variances both HH and the gap are 0 throughout. vignette("implementation") gives the argument.

The concentration count

With the proportions qj=Sj/∑kSkq_j = S_j / \sum_k S_k of the total reliability, the concentration count is the inverse of the sum of their squares,

Jeff=(∑jSj)2∑jSj2=1∑jqj2. J_{\mathrm{eff}} = \frac{(\sum_j S_j)^2}{\sum_j S_j^2} = \frac{1}{\sum_j q_j^2}.

Its largest value, JJ, belongs to profiles of equally reliable sites, and it approaches 1, without reaching it, as one site’s proportion approaches 1. It depends only on the proportions. A trial whose 40 sites all have reliability 0.05 and one whose 40 sites all have 0.95 both have Jeff=40J_{\mathrm{eff}} = 40.

We plot the cumulative proportions of the two concentrated profiles, the most reliable sites first, with plot() and type = "concentration", a call to plot_concentration(). Because the 8 precise sites are tied, we leave out the labels that would name the most reliable sites.

plot(two, type = "concentration", label_top = 0)

With 8 precise sites the curve climbs steeply over the first fifth of the sites, which carry 52% of the total reliability, and then rises slowly. With 8 noisy sites it climbs evenly, a little faster than the diagonal, until the 32 precise sites have contributed 98% of the total, and the 8 noisy ones add the rest. The concentration counts printed in the panel, 24.1 and 33.3, summarize the two curves. To see which sites carry the reliability in your own analysis, you can give a posterior fit to plot_concentration() and plot_contributions() as well.

The geometry in two plots

Each site’s term of HH is a Bregman divergence. With ϕ(p)=plog⁡p+(1−p)log⁡(1−p)\phi(p) = p \log p + (1 - p)\log(1 - p), the term KL{Ber(I)∥Ber(Sj)}\mathrm{KL}\{\mathrm{Ber}(I) \,\|\, \mathrm{Ber}(S_j)\} is the height of ϕ\phi at II above the tangent to ϕ\phi at SjS_j. plot_geometry() shows the curve, the tangents at a few sites and these heights. We use the even profile, whose 40 reliabilities all differ, and four of its sites spread over the range.

even <- profiles$even
plot_geometry(even, sites = c(1, 14, 27, 40))

In panel (a) the longest gap belongs to the most reliable of the four sites, at 0.77, and the next longest to the least reliable, at 0.05. These two sites are equally far from II on the logit scale, but the divergence is not symmetric, and the site above II has the larger term. Between them, the sites at 0.46 and 0.18 are closer to II and have short gaps. Panel (b) gives the four terms as bars, 0.503, 0.054, 0.045 and 0.317. Their mean is not HH, the average over all 40 sites.

Theorem 2 of Lee (2026) splits the average divergence of a constant reliability pp from the profile into two parts,

1J∑j=1JKL{Ber(p)∥Ber(Sj)}=KL{Ber(p)∥Ber(I)}+H, \frac{1}{J}\sum_{j=1}^J \mathrm{KL}\{\mathrm{Ber}(p) \,\|\, \mathrm{Ber}(S_j)\} = \mathrm{KL}\{\mathrm{Ber}(p) \,\|\, \mathrm{Ber}(I)\} + H,

so the average is smallest at p=Ip = I, where it equals HH. plot_decomposition() plots the left side against pp and shows the split at one value of pp, here 0.75.

plot_decomposition(even, at = 0.75)

The curve’s minimum, at I=0.3I = 0.3, is H=0.149H = 0.149, the height of the dashed line. At p=0.75p = 0.75 the average divergence is 0.578, of which 0.430 is the divergence of 0.75 from II and the rest is HH. The mean reliability, 0.347, sits just to the right of the minimum and a little above it on the curve. It minimizes the average with pp in the second argument, a different function of pp.

Making profiles of your own

You can build profiles like these with shape_profile(), for a simulation or to see what the diagnostics of a planned trial might look like. It returns sampling variances with a given number of sites, informativeness, logit variance and shape at a given στ\sigma_\tau. Here we ask for 20 sites in two groups, with I=1/2I = 1/2 and V=1V = 1.

v <- shape_profile(J = 20, I = 0.5, V = 1, shape = "bimodal",
                   sigma_tau = 0.25)
half <- reliability_profile(se2 = v, sigma_tau = 0.25)
half
#> Reliability profile of 20 sites at sigma_tau = 0.25 (supplied)
#> 
#>   informativeness I            0.500
#>   mean reliability             0.500
#>   dispersion H                 0.1201
#>   logit variance V             1.000
#>   concentration count J_eff    16.5 of 20
#> 
#> Site reliabilities range from 0.27 to 0.73.

Its reliabilities take two values, 0.27 and 0.73, whose logits lie symmetrically around logitI=0\mathrm{logit}\, I = 0. At I=1/2I = 1/2 the gap’s leading term is 0, and for this symmetric profile the mean reliability equals II. Yet H=0.120H = 0.120, close to its leading term 12I(1−I)V=0.125\tfrac12 I(1 - I)V = 0.125, so two equal centroids do not make the reliabilities equal.

vignette("planning") starts instead from the site sizes, and vignette("posterior-summaries") returns to an estimated στ\sigma_\tau.

References

Lee, JoonHo. 2026. “The Geometry of Informativeness: A Bregman-Centroid Diagnostic for Partial Pooling in Multisite Trials.” Unpublished manuscript.
